title: Chapter 5 Test: B2B Wholesale
description: Eighteen questions on the company and catalog model, B2B theme development, wholesale ordering UX, payment terms and draft orders, and extending B2B with Functions. Aim for 75%.

questions.prompt: In Shopify's native B2B model, at what level is pricing resolved?
options: The company
The company location
The company contact
The customer tag
questions.explanation: Catalogs are assigned to company locations, so a company's Manchester branch can be on a different tier from its head office. This is not an edge case — it is how distribution businesses work, and it is the reason a tag-based wholesale implementation cannot be retrofitted.

questions.prompt: A distributor has negotiated 35% off boots, 20% off gloves, and an extra 5% at 24 or more of any SKU. How should this be modelled?
options: A discount Function reading a customer tag
A catalog price list with percentage adjustments and quantity price breaks, assigned to that company's locations
Two discount codes
A separate expansion store
questions.explanation: These are prices, not promotions. A price list shows the correct price on the product page rather than revealing it at checkout, avoids a struck-through DTC price that reads as a consumer sale, and is scoped to exactly the entitled locations.

questions.prompt: Native B2B can be enabled on a store still using the classic customer account system.
questions.explanation: B2B requires the newer customer accounts — the classic system has nowhere for company context to live. On an inherited store, migrating accounts is a prerequisite for B2B, not an optional modernisation, and it changes login flows and account page work entirely.

questions.prompt: Which are true of quantity rules in a B2B catalog? Select all that apply.
options: They set minimum, maximum and increment per variant
They are enforced by the platform in cart and checkout
Your theme should surface them before the buyer hits them
They are applied per company rather than per catalog
questions.explanation: Rules live on the catalog and are enforced platform-side. The theme's job is to make them visible in advance — feeding min, max and step into the quantity input — which is the difference between a good wholesale experience and an irritating one.

questions.prompt: A buyer with 40 cart lines switches company location. What must the theme do?
options: Nothing — Shopify remaps the cart with correct prices
Warn before switching, then verify the cart afterwards, because catalogs, prices and quantity rules can differ per location
Silently clear the cart
Block switching whenever the cart is not empty
questions.explanation: Availability, price and rules resolve per location. Silently repricing a 40-line order destroys trust; clearing it destroys twenty minutes of work. Warn, switch, verify, and report exactly what changed.

questions.prompt: Why should a trade buyer not see a struck-through compare-at price?
options: Liquid cannot render compare-at prices for B2B customers
Their catalog price is their price — a compare-at implies a temporary sale, frames a contract relationship wrongly, and exposes consumer margin
Compare-at prices break quantity price breaks
It is prohibited by Shopify's terms
questions.explanation: This is a merchandising judgement with a commercial edge. Trade accounts have prices; consumers get deals. Showing the DTC price also tells a buyer exactly what your consumer margin is, which they will remember at the next negotiation.

questions.prompt: A quick order grid collects quantities for 40 variants. How should it add them to the cart?
options: One /cart/add.js request per line, sequentially
One /cart/add.js request containing an items array
Forty parallel requests
A form POST to /cart per line
questions.explanation: A single request with an items array is one round trip, avoids rate limiting, and cannot leave a partial cart the buyer has to reconcile. Per-line errors come back identified, so you show them against the offending row.

questions.prompt: A buyer pastes 60 SKUs; four are unrecognised and two exceed stock. What is the right behaviour?
options: Reject the whole submission
Add the 54 valid lines and report each problem line with a specific reason, allowing resubmission of only those
Add all 60 and let checkout reject them
Add the valid lines with a generic 'some items failed' message
questions.explanation: Rejecting everything wastes 54 correct lines; a generic message leaves the buyer guessing which six and why. Per-line status with a specific reason is what makes bulk entry usable rather than a novelty.

questions.prompt: Order these wholesale channel phases by the sequence that produces adoption before control.
items: Commercial rules — minimums, credit limits, freight rules
Foundations — companies, catalogs, price lists, terms
Automation — provisioning, tier changes, price updates
Ordering efficiency — quick order, bulk entry, saved lists, reorder
answer: Foundations — companies, catalogs, price lists, terms
Ordering efficiency — quick order, bulk entry, saved lists, reorder
Commercial rules — minimums, credit limits, freight rules
Automation — provisioning, tier changes, price updates
questions.explanation: Commercial rules enforced on a storefront buyers do not use are enforcement against nobody. Adoption first, control second, automation once volume justifies it.

questions.prompt: Which Flow trigger silently stops working when payment terms are introduced?
options: Order created
Order paid
Company created
Product published
questions.explanation: A terms order is created without payment, so anything keyed on payment never fires — with no error and no alert, just orders quietly not reaching the warehouse. Auditing every automation, integration and report keyed on payment is the single most important B2B launch task.

questions.prompt: What can a draft order do that a storefront checkout cannot? Select all that apply.
options: Include custom line items with no SKU, such as a setup fee
Override pricing for a one-off negotiated order
Send an invoice the buyer pays later
Enforce theme-side JavaScript validation
questions.explanation: Draft orders bypass the storefront entirely, which is exactly why theme-side validation does not apply to them. Anything commercially meaningful belongs in a cart and checkout validation Function.

questions.prompt: A £500 trade minimum is enforced by JavaScript in the cart. A rep creates a £300 draft order. What happens?
options: It is rejected because minimums apply account-wide
It proceeds — theme validation does not apply to draft orders, the API, or POS
Shopify enforces it automatically once a company is attached
The buyer is blocked at the invoice payment page
questions.explanation: Theme validation runs only in the theme. Knowing which of your rules are platform-enforced and which are theme-enforced — and being able to state that list — is a genuine architectural artefact.

questions.prompt: Where should a per-account free-carriage threshold live?
options: Hard-coded in the shipping discount Function
In a company metafield read by the Function's input query
In a theme setting
In a discount code issued to the account
questions.explanation: A metafield makes the threshold data rather than code: sales ops changes it per account with no deployment, and one Function serves every account. This is the same principle as schema settings and Function configuration metafields, applied to the account layer.

questions.prompt: A Shopify Function can call an external API at run time to check a live credit balance.
questions.explanation: Functions have no network access. The balance must already be on the store — synced into a company metafield by an integration — which means it carries latency. Design for a soft warning threshold plus a hard block some way above it, and say so up front.

questions.prompt: Match each B2B need to the right mechanism.

pairs.left: Minimum order value that holds on draft orders too
Hide parcel carriers for a freight-only account
Notify the assigned rep of a large order

questions.explanation: Prices are catalogs, rules are Functions, reactions are Flow. Mixing these up — usually by expressing pricing as a discount or enforcement as theme code — produces most of the defects in a wholesale implementation.

questions.prompt: Which Liquid boolean tells you the logged-in customer is shopping in a B2B company context?
questions.explanation: `customer.b2b?` is only meaningful when a customer is logged in — a guest correctly sees DTC pricing. That has a consequence worth designing for: a trade buyer who is not signed in sees consumer prices, so the sign-in prompt should be specific rather than generic.

questions.prompt: Why is the "consumed by" column in a metafield inventory particularly valuable on a Shopify platform?
options: Shopify requires documented metafields
A single metafield can be read by Liquid, a Function, a Flow workflow, a POS extension and an integration, so without it every field is load-bearing in unknown ways
It improves storefront performance
It is needed to enable storefront access
questions.explanation: Deleting or changing a definition destroys every value with no undo. The inventory is what makes a field safe to touch — and it has to be filled in as you build, because the documentation sprint afterwards never happens.

questions.prompt: Before running a bulk price list update on a live wholesale catalog, what is the most important precaution?
options: Running it outside business hours
Exporting the current price list first as a rollback, and verifying the result as a logged-in buyer rather than from the admin
Increasing the API rate limit
Notifying Shopify support
questions.explanation: A wrong wholesale price can produce orders you are commercially obliged to honour. The export is the rollback; verifying as a buyer is the only way to see what the customer actually pays, because the admin shows configuration rather than the resolved price.
